articles.title: 'Told them to give it to me in writing': Raihan Vadra recounts how events unfolded before photos were taken down at Bikaner House exhibition
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Artist and photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra, has detailed his interactions with
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Artist and photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra, has detailed his interactions with Bikaner House officials over the removal of photographs depicting youth protests in Delhi from his exhibition, alleging that the administration gave him only a few hours to comply with its objections.Speaking about the controversy, Raihan said his solo exhibition, titled No Idea Is Fine, was scheduled to open at 7 pm, but the venue's management raised objections to some of the photographs shortly before the event.He alleged that officials subsequently insisted that all 70 images be removed, including photographs featuring the Indian national flag.Speaking to news agency ANI, Raihan said the Bikaner House management first contacted him 24 hours before the scheduled opening and told him that some images violated its policy. He said he asked the officials to identify the photographs and discuss their objections, but did not receive a response until the following day.He said the deputy resident commissioner later contacted him and instructed him to remove the photographs, which documented youth movements in Delhi over the preceding year.“I said, 'I shared the layout a week earlier; why didn't you bring it up earlier?' They said, 'We couldn't see the layout.' So I said, 'You still had 1 week to tell me you couldn't see the layout. I would have sent it; we could have had the discussion earlier. Now, in 4-5 hours, what am I going to do?'” Raihan said.Officials allegedly refused to provide written explanationRaihan said he asked the management to provide written explanations for the removal of individual photographs but did not receive them.He said the principal resident commissioner subsequently visited the exhibition at around 3 pm and reiterated the objections. According to Raihan, the official cited the venue's policy against political content.Raihan said he had already removed most photographs featuring political parties and leaders and was willing to replace any remaining images that violated the policy.“For the most part, I had removed imagery of political parties and of political leaders. Maybe there were a few photographs; I said, 'We could discuss. If they are against your policy, I'll replace them.' He said, 'No, none of these 70 images will be put up,'” he said.According to Raihan, the management issued a notice at 3.30 pm warning that the building would be sealed and the exhibition cancelled if the photographs were not removed by 5 pm.He said he initially complied by turning the framed photographs around so that only their backs were visible. However, he alleged that officials objected to this arrangement as well, prompting him to take the frames down and move them into storage.Dispute over photographs of the TricolourRaihan said he left two photographs featuring the Indian flag on display, arguing that they could not reasonably violate the venue's policy. He alleged that officials asked him to remove them but did not provide a written order when he requested one.“I said, 'This can't be against your policy. How can it be against your policy?' I said, 'Give it to me in writing that you want me to take down a picture of the Indian flag.' They didn't,” he said.Raihan added that he left the venue to change clothes and that officials removed one of the two photographs themselves. One image of the national flag remained on display, he said.In an earlier statement, Raihan had said he would not remove the photographs featuring the Tricolour and that the exhibition would proceed in a limited capacity while he looked for an alternative venue to display the complete collection.The controversy drew reactions from members of the Congress. Priyanka Gandhi Vadra backed her son in a post on X, writing, “When someone with power becomes afraid of the expression of another, he doesn’t know it, but he has already lost the very power he is trying to protect. You stand for what is true and everything beautiful will find its way to you. I am proud of you, always will be.”Robert Vadra also shared his son's statement, while Congress MP Karti Chidambaram criticised the Bikaner House administration's conduct.Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pawan Khera alleged that the removal of the photographs amounted to censorship.In a post on X, he said the works documented protests and questioned why images of demonstrations, including the national flag, had become objectionable.The exhibition, No Idea Is Fine, was scheduled to open at Bikaner House on Thursday evening.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Foyil is a small town in Rogers County, in northeastern Oklahoma. Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park sits on Oklahoma State Highway 28A, east of town and near Route 66, the historic road connecting Claremore and Tulsa. Travelers who took the turnoff found themselves on a farm that looked quite different from the surrounding fields and grassland. A group of painted concrete sculptures stands on the land, including a totem pole that towers over the surrounding trees. After his retirement to a farm that he and his wife had been cultivating for years, he undertook a project that would consume the rest of his life.Ed Galloway’s move to the Foyil farm The National Park Service states that Galloway was born in 1880 in Springfield, Missouri and later worked at Sand Springs Home, where he taught manual arts to orphaned boys. He purchased the property near Foyil along with his wife, Villie, in the early 1920s, as explained in the Rogers County Historical Society biography of his life. The National Park Service page on Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park, a National Register of Historic Places entry, records that he retired to that property in 1937. The Spaces Archives notes that Galloway began creating large sculptures from tree trunks, incorporating human figures, fish and reptiles into the carvings.One of those early trunk pieces, shown in the archive photographs reproduced in the NPS paper Restoration of Ed Galloway’s Totem Pole Park, sits on the back of a turtle. The paper notes that Galloway later reused that turtle motif for the tall concrete pole. The paper gives the larger context behind that detail, noting that the trunk sculpture appears in an archive postcard and that the turtle base became a recurring structural idea in Galloway’s later concrete work. It also places the piece within his early wood-carving period, before he shifted to the massive concrete totem that rose over the sandstone outcrop.An eleven-year build from 1937 to 1948 using 28 tons of cementAccording to Legends of America, Galloway erected the pole in eleven years between 1937 and 1948, using 28 tons of cement, six tons of steel and 100 tons of sand and rock. According to Oklahoma Magazine, the hollow pole stands on a sandstone formation, which was found at the site of the pole and which Galloway sculpted into a turtle due to its resemblance to one. According to the NPS web page, the pole passes through nine stories, with the ground story being nine feet wide. Its height is also inconsistent. The most common height of the pole is 90 feet, as claimed by the NPS web page and the Historical Society, although preservation literature offers lower measurements, such as 78 feet.More than 200 carved figures arranged toward the four directionsThe restoration paper talks about more than two hundred hand-carved bas-relief animals and portrait busts on the pole. There are four nine-foot-high portraits at the top of the pole; these include portraits of Quanah Parker, Sitting Bull, Geronimo and Chief Joseph. The NPS page says that the sculptures usually depict birds and figures of Northwest Coast, Alaska and Plains cultures. The decorations are generally oriented towards the four cardinal directions. His source material was quite mundane. The NPS page says that Galloway used postcards and National Geographic magazines as his source material for the faces and symbols that he carved onto the wet concrete and then painted.Decline after Galloway’s death The date of death varies between sources, with the NPS citing 1961 and the restoration paper citing 1962. The park started deteriorating after that time. According to the restoration paper, restoration work of the park started in the early 1980s under the Kansas Grassroots Art Association, while NPS cites 1988 through 1998 as the period for major restoration work.By around 1989, ownership of the park had passed to the Rogers County Historical Society, according to the society’s information on the Totem Pole Park website. Maintenance arrangements under the society continued to change into the early 1990s. The landmark was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1999. According to Legends of America, the Foyil Heritage Society is also involved in fundraising and groundskeeping.Mineral silicate paint applied in two layers during the restorationRestoration paper by the National Park Service shows that the restoration of the deteriorated paint of the poles was done through the use of mineral silicate paint. The upper part of the pole received painting in two layers, while the bottom twenty-five feet was left for a later phase of work. Silicate paint was used because it was resistant to water and algae and did not peel or fade. According to the page on the NPS website, it is the oldest and largest folk art environment in Oklahoma. There are fourteen other concrete sculptures around the main pole, including the bird gateposts, totem picnic tables and fish-shaped arch. According to the Legends of America, the eleven-sided Fiddle House is where Galloway showcased his handcrafted fiddles and furniture.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: Acer has launched TravelLite TL44-53M-G2, a new premium 14-inch business notebook that comes powered by the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors and Intel vPro platform. The notebook measures less than 18 mm thin and weighs under 1.4 kg for easy mobility. It has a 14-inch FHD IPS display offering 300-nit brightness and a 16:10 aspect ratio, providing ample workspace for business applications. It has a 180-degree lay-flat hinge that enables flexible collaboration and content sharing, while the narrow-bezel design adds a premium appearance. The TravelLite is also MIL-STD 810H certified.The new Acer notebook features a 5MP IR camera for enhanced video quality and Windows Hello biometric authentication. Combined with stereo speakers, DTS® Audio and noise-cancelling microphones, it delivers clearer, more immersive virtual meetings, presentations and everyday collaboration.Connectivity features include two USB Type-C ports with Thunderbolt, DisplayPort and USB charging. Its dual M.2 PCIe NVMe SSD slots, including PCIe 5.0 x4 support, deliver high-speed storage performance and future expansion flexibility. For wireless connectivity, configurations support Intel Wi-Fi 7 (BE211) 2×2 and Bluetooth 5.4, alongside Intel vPro platform capabilities.The TravelLite TL44-53M-G2 support for up to 128GB of dual-channel DDR5 memory and dual M.2 storage enables organizations to configure systems for diverse employee roles and workload requirements.Commenting on the launch, Sudhir Goel, Chief Business Officer, Acer India, said, “The expectations from a business PC have fundamentally changed. Enterprises today need devices that combine intelligent performance with strong security, manageability, and an experience employees genuinely want to use. With the new TravelLite, we are bringing together Acer's premium commercial design with the latest Intel ®Core™ Ultra Series 3 and Intel vPro® platform capabilities to address these needs. It is a device designed not only for the way businesses work today, but for the increasingly AI-enabled workplace they are building for tomorrow.”GS Sondhi, Senior Director, Product Management, Acer India, said, “In developing the TravelLite TL44-53M-G2, our focus was on the practical needs of both business users and IT teams. IT teams need security, manageability, and flexibility to support changing business requirements. By combining AI-ready performance with a durable, lightweight design, expandable memory and storage, and reliable battery life, the new TravelLite gives enterprises a platform that can grow with their needs.”The Acer TravelLite TL44-53M-G2 will be available in India through Acer's commercial and enterprise channels. articles.title: From 1968 to 1977, retired North Carolina tobacco farmer Henry Warren built a 27-building miniature stone village around a large metal water tower
articles.summary: Explore the captivating story of Henry Warren, a retired tobacco farmer who, in 1968, initiated the construction of a whimsical stone village called Shangri-La in North Carolina. Discover the village's unique buildings, materials, and the legacy it left behind after Warren's passing in 1977.
articles.body: Caswell County lies along the northern edge of North Carolina’s Piedmont, in a region where tobacco was a major cash crop for generations. State Highway 86 runs through the county and passes near the unincorporated community of Prospect Hill. Hidden off the road, next to a volunteer fire station, is a grouping of little houses constructed from white rocks, quartz, bricks and cement, about as tall as a person. The little town does not have a fee or even a ticket booth for entrance; entry is free to all who visit. It was constructed by hand by a retired farmer on his property. The information provided herein deals with the man’s background, motivations, creations and post-death situation.Henry Warren’s retirement from farming Henry L. Warren was a Caswell County native who farmed tobacco until he retired. Our State magazine reports that he began the village in 1968 at age 75 and spent the last nine years of his life on it. The age of 75 fits a death at 84 in 1977, as Roadside America records, whereas VisitNC’s figure of 72 would make him 81 at his death and does not match that record. The Carrboro Citizen column Just Down the Road in Shangri-La describes the village as a hobby that developed over nine years and records that Warren died in 1977. The column references a story from The State magazine from 1979, titled “The Little Stone Village of Prospect Hill,” about a small village made of rocks and mortar and containing over 20 structures. Quoting from Our State, this project came about for the simple reason that farmers were accustomed to working with their hands and needed to have something to do after retirement.A miniature waterwheel from a Hillsborough antiques shopOur State also ties the village to a miniature waterwheel that Warren spotted at an antiques shop in Hillsborough. The magazine notes, “Some of his neighbors referred to it as White Rock Village, but he preferred the name Shangri-La.” The wheel was part of Warren’s completed village, which ABC11 describes as a collection of buildings surrounding a large metal water tower and pond.White flint rock blasted from the family property Roadside America describes how Warren quarried solid rock from his own property and worked on the village from dawn until dusk. Our State mentions white flint rock, quartz, red brick and cement as some of the materials that were used, while the steeple of the church is described as an inverted table leg painted white.According to Atlas Obscura, the stone pathway through the village is one of his inventions. Roadside America states that the total number of arrowheads embedded in the pathways is 11,000, while Atlas Obscura just mentions that there are thousands. ABC11 describes the winding pathway made of quartz, stones and arrowheads passing through tall bushes. Warren’s wife told Roadside America that as long as he had a cigarette and a Coke, he kept building.27 buildings standing at Warren’s death in 1977ABC11 and Roadside America both count 27 buildings in the village at the time of Warren’s death. Our State lists a church, hospital, mill, motel, movie theater, general store, jail, library, city hall and even a liquor store and Atlas Obscura adds a gym and a hotel. A bank and a gas station round out the list in Roadside America’s account and the Carrboro Citizen also places a fire station among them. The buildings stand about five feet tall, as ABC11 and VisitNC measure them. Visitors can also rest on carved thrones and feel like kings or queens of the village, a detail ABC11 highlights.The 1972 plaque and the hospital Warren was working on in 1977In 1972, Warren engraved his motto on a stone slab, ABC11 reports, reading: “Let me live in the house by the side of the road and be a friend to man.” Roadside America notes that a sign bearing the same inscription is found at the front of his house. The same source reports that Warren died of cancer in 1977 while still at work on the village’s miniature hospital. Whether that hospital was ever finished is unclear, since WRAL and Atlas Obscura both count 27 completed structures at the time of his death.Warren’s wife and daughter and the village’s upkeep As summarized in the North Carolina Periodicals Index entry for the 1979 magazine article, his wife eventually gave free tours of the village to visitors, with children and older people coming most often. According to ABC11, currently, Warren’s daughter and her family preserve Shangri-La. In addition, the journal of visitors, which is located on a grass-covered hill above the village, contains decades of thank-you messages to the Warren family. The stone/concrete construction has contributed to the durability of the buildings, as noted by Atlas Obscura and visitors can still use the trail from the house to the village.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, 80 runners covered 230 km of Kenyan wilderness over five race stages within an eight-day event; the ForRangers Ultra raised more than £125,000 for wildlife rangers
articles.summary: In 2025, eighty daring runners traversed 230 km of rugged Kenyan terrain, raising £125,000 for the dedicated rangers protecting endangered wildlife in the ForRangers Ultra race.
articles.body: The Laikipia region of central Kenya sits on a high plateau northwest of Mount Kenya and much of it is divided into wildlife conservancies. These places are home to rhinos, elephants, zebras, giraffes and many other animals and are guarded by rangers who try to ensure that no poachers can enter their territory. The area is very rugged and the interior of the conservancies is rarely seen by anyone but locals. Every year, athletes take part in a long-distance foot race across these conservancies. Called the ForRangers Ultra, it is a self-sufficient event and the money it raises goes toward ranger welfare and rhino conservation.The first race in 2018 drew about 50 runnersThe race began in 2018 with about 50 runners, as Beyond the Ultimate and Big Life both report, although Save the Rhino’s event page puts the figure at more than 40. The event is a collaboration between Save the Rhino, ForRangers and Beyond the Ultimate. The first edition covered 220 km, 10 km shorter than the 230 km course of 2025. Hundreds of people have taken part so far and the event website describes the race as a way to connect participants with rhino conservation at its core and with the people they are helping.80 runners leaving the foothills of Mount KenyaThe Save the Rhino diary, titled “The 2025 ForRangers Ultra Race Diary: £125,000 raised for Kenya’s Rangers,” opens on a sunny September morning in the shadow of Mount Kenya. A field of 80 runners set off on a 230 km course. The diary was written by Eleanor Glynne-Jones, the charity’s Michael Hearn intern and Raj Pandya, its community fundraising manager.Five stages in five days through five conservanciesAs seen in the mentioned diary, the duration of the course is five days. From the description given at Beyond the Ultimate, the structure is five stages in five days in an event that lasts eight days, with arrival and recovery times included. As noted on the event page, the route traverses five conservancies with varied landscapes, ranging from savannah to thick forests and goes through the foothills of Mount Kenya up to the equator.Carrying food, safety gear and at least 2.5 litres of waterThe fundraising page for the 2025 race describes the event as completely self-contained. Each runner carried their own food, safety equipment and at least 2.5 litres of water, which could be replenished at checkpoints and camped in the wilderness every night. Helicopters, aircraft, and rangers provided support, according to Beyond the Ultimate and the runners shared the course with rhinos, elephants, impalas, zebras and giraffes.Runners and Laikipia rangers on the same courseThe diary notes that for the five days, runners from all over the world ran beside, spoke to and were safeguarded by rangers from the Laikipia area. Each of the runners received a Save the Rhino wristband with one simple directive: give it to a ranger at some point during the 230 km run.As noted by Glynne-Jones, the participants were consistently grateful to both the rangers and the medical team for the duration of five days. Beyond the Ultimate frames the wider conservation effort more sharply, describing the struggle as a war between organised poachers and the rangers protecting the animals.More than £125,000 raised for ranger welfare and rhino conservationTogether, the diary says, the runners helped raise over £125,000 for rangers in Kenya. The diary explains how the money is used. It supports the rangers and conservancies that the runners travel through, giving them equipment, training and facilities that allow the rangers to protect animals and their habitat. It adds that the funds also support the conservation of all five rhino species.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Woman pays Rs 1,100 for facial laser hair removal but says the treatment left her with burns and darkened skin; Bengaluru consumer commission finds deficiency and orders Rs 1.11 lakh payout, with interest on refund
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Bengaluru district consumer commission has held a beauty clinic liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Bengaluru district consumer commission has held a beauty clinic liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman suffered facial burns following a laser hair removal procedure. The commission directed the clinic to pay Rs 1.1 lakh in damages and litigation costs, besides refunding the procedure fee with interest.In its September 30, 2026, order, the III Additional Bengaluru Urban District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission directed the clinic to refund Rs 1,100 with interest from the date of payment until realisation, pay Rs 1 lakh as damages for skin damage and mental agony, and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. It gave the clinic 45 days to comply.Laser hair removal procedure leaves woman with facial burnsAccording to the commission order, Anitha, a resident of Bengaluru, visited Berkowits Hair & Skin Clinic on April 22, 2026, for a scheduled laser hair removal session on her upper lip and chin. She paid Rs 1,100 for the procedure.During the treatment, she experienced an intense burning sensation and informed the technician about her discomfort. The technician allegedly told her that the sensation was normal and continued with the procedure.The woman said she suffered severe burns and inflammation on her lip and chin immediately after the session. Her skin later became extremely dark, and she developed a painful wound that was identified as a second-degree burn, according to the complaint.She subsequently consulted doctors at other branches of the clinic for further treatment. She also alleged that the injuries affected her facial appearance, confidence and professional life.Anitha sent a legal notice to the clinic on April 26, 2026, seeking compensation. The clinic replied on April 30, denying liability. She then approached the consumer commission, seeking a refund of the procedure fee, Rs 3 lakh in compensation and Rs 25,000 towards litigation costs.The clinic contested the allegations in its written arguments, denying deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. It also argued that the complaint was liable to be dismissed on grounds relating to the parties included in the case. The commission, however, rejected the clinic's formal version on September 7, 2026, because it had been filed beyond the statutory period, though it retained the document on record.Commission's finding on laser hair removal treatmentThe commission, comprising president Shivaram K and members Rekha Sayannavar and Suma Anilkumar, examined the woman's evidence, photographs of her facial injuries, medical prescription and correspondence between the parties.It noted that the woman had produced photographs showing burn injuries and a medical prescription relating to further treatment. The commission also considered her allegation that the clinic had failed to conduct an adequate preliminary assessment of her skin and a necessary sensitivity test before proceeding with the treatment.The commission held that a service provider carrying out a cosmetic procedure directly on the skin was required to exercise reasonable care, including making appropriate enquiries about the customer's skin condition, allergies and possible contraindications.It observed that the clinic's failure to take the necessary precautions amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.The commission also considered the impact of the injuries on the woman's appearance and confidence, noting that she had approached the clinic to improve her appearance but instead suffered a visible adverse reaction.Final orderThe commission partly allowed the complaint and directed Berkowits Hair & Skin Clinic to:Refund Rs 1,100 with 9 percent annual interest from the date of payment until realisation.Pay Rs 1 lakh as damages for skin damage and mental agony.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The clinic was directed to comply with the order within 45 days. If it fails to do so, the amount of Rs 1.1 lakh will carry interest at 9 percent per annum from the date of the order until realisation.The total fixed payout ordered by the commission is Rs 1.11 lakh, excluding interest on the refund and any additional interest that may apply in case of non-compliance.

articles.title: A 17-year-old North Carolina soldier killed in the Korean War and buried for decades as Unknown X-1642 is being laid to rest in Maryland,  more than 70 years later, after DNA analysis finally identified him
articles.summary: A US Army private who was killed during the Korean War at just 17 years old is finally being laid to rest under his own name, more than seven decades
articles.body: A US Army private who was killed during the Korean War at just 17 years old is finally being laid to rest under his own name, more than seven decades after his remains were buried as an unidentified soldier. Pvt. Joseph E. Boyd, from Bear Creek, North Carolina, was identified after forensic scientists analysed remains designated “Unknown X-1642”, according to the US Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA). The agency announced on October 17, 2026, that Boyd had been accounted for on June 10, with his burial scheduled for October 21 in Owings Mills, Maryland.Boyd was serving with Company A, 1st Battalion, 9th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, when he was reported missing on January 25, 1951, near Chigu-ri, South Korea. His disappearance occurred during patrol operations as US forces fought to clear enemy troops from mountainous areas near Wonju. His remains were not recovered at the time, leaving his fate unresolved for decades.Remains recovered but identity remained unknownIn February 1951, a local villager discovered human remains near Saemal, South Korea. A US Army search-and-recovery team retrieved them and transferred them to the Central Identification Unit in Kokura, Japan, for examination. Despite the identification methods available at the time, investigators could not establish the person's identity.The remains were designated “Unknown X-1642 Tanggok” and, in 1956, were buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. The cemetery, commonly known as the Punchbowl, became the final resting place for hundreds of unidentified American service members from the Korean War. Boyd's remains remained there for decades without his name being attached to them.The identification effort was part of a broader programme to resolve cases involving American service members whose remains had been recovered but could not be identified using the scientific techniques available at the time. In 2018, the DPAA proposed a plan to disinter 652 Korean War unknowns from the Punchbowl for renewed examination.As part of the programme, officials exhumed Unknown X-1642 in November 2023 and transferred the remains to a DPAA laboratory for further analysis. The renewed examination allowed specialists to compare the remains with records and evidence associated with service members who had been reported missing during the conflict.How scientists identified BoydThe identification relied on several forms of evidence rather than DNA testing alone. According to the DPAA, scientists combined dental and anthropological analysis with circumstantial evidence. Specialists from the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System also used mitochondrial DNA analysis and mitochondrial genome sequencing data to help establish the identity.The process illustrates how advances in forensic science can help resolve cases that remained uncertain for generations. Dental comparisons and anthropological examinations can help narrow the list of possible identities, while genetic analysis can provide additional evidence when suitable reference samples are available from relatives.The DPAA's wider disinterment programme involves researchers examining historical records, personnel files, unit documents and reports of earlier investigations alongside laboratory findings. Investigators compare the circumstances in which unidentified remains were recovered with the documented disappearance of missing service members. When the evidence indicates a likely match, the remains can be exhumed for detailed forensic analysis.Boyd's identification was announced after his family received a full briefing from officials, allowing the agency to release further details about the case.A wider effort to identify the missingBoyd's case forms part of a continuing US effort to account for military personnel who went missing in past conflicts. According to the DPAA, more than 7,000 Americans remain unaccounted for from the Korean War, and the agency continues to investigate possible recovery sites and examine unidentified remains.The Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953, left families across the United States without definitive answers about relatives who never returned. Some remains were recovered during or shortly after the fighting, but the methods available then were not always sufficient to identify them. Those remains were often buried as unknowns, with the possibility of future identification left open.The DPAA says its ongoing work combines historical research, field investigations and laboratory techniques, including DNA analysis, to provide families with answers where possible. The disinterment programme also allows officials to revisit remains that had previously been considered unidentifiable.Burial more than seven decades laterBoyd's name had been recorded among the missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Following his identification, the DPAA said a rosette would be placed next to his name at the Courts of the Missing to indicate that he had been accounted for. His burial was scheduled for October 21, 2026, in Owings Mills, Maryland.For a soldier who disappeared at 17, the identification brings an official resolution to a case that remained open for more than 75 years. The forensic work cannot recover the time his family spent without knowing what happened to him, but it has restored his identity to remains that had long been recorded only by a number.Boyd's case also demonstrates why the search for missing service members continues decades after a conflict ends. As forensic techniques improve and old records are revisited, remains once buried without names can sometimes be returned to families for burial with the recognition they were denied for generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka seek more time, skip Delhi Police questioning
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka will not appear before the Delhi Police Crime Branch for questioning on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka will not appear before the Delhi Police Crime Branch for questioning on Thursday after seeking more time, sources told ANI. Police are expected to issue a fresh notice to the two leaders, the sources said.The Crime Branch had summoned Das and Ranka to its Rajouri Garden office on Thursday, a day after they were released from judicial custody.The two were released after a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court accepted their personal and surety bonds and recorded their written undertakings to maintain peace and abide by the law.SEM Ritu Raj directed them to furnish personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the enquiry. They were also instructed to appear on every hearing date and comply with the conditions specified in their bonds and undertakings.In their written undertakings, the leaders promised not to breach peace or disturb public tranquillity. They also agreed not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law, and said any future demonstrations would be held within the constitutional framework.The two leaders were detained in connection with an October 13 protest at Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a designated protest site. Police alleged that they entered the area through private premises and violated conditions related to maintaining peace.The Delhi Police had earlier sought a further three-day extension of their judicial custody, citing concerns over a possible breach of peace and law and order. Police also pointed to alleged differences between statements made by the leaders before the court and their subsequent remarks to the media.The matter is scheduled for further proceedings before the SEM court on October 23 at 3 pm. Das, Ranka and their sureties have been directed to remain present.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia on Thursday questioned Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s alleged links with foreign-based organisations,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia on Thursday questioned Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s alleged links with foreign-based organisations, including Progressive International and Indian Alliance Paris, accusing them of amplifying protests in India and alleging a wider conspiracy to create “anarchy and chaos” in the country.Addressing a press conference, Bhatia repeatedly referred to Gandhi as “Rahul Gaddar” and alleged that the Congress leadership’s engagement with international groups raised questions about their activities, funding and possible coordination with protests in India. His remarks followed a Fox News Digital investigation that claimed to have identified 101 organisations across nine countries involved in organising, coordinating or amplifying demonstrations.“The subject is the model of anarchy, chaos, and treachery that the Leader of the Opposition, Rahul Gandhi, is presenting before the country. Now, a news report was published in a very prestigious newspaper today, regarding how these threads of treachery are connecting with foreign agencies,” Bhatia said.“If it is asked, who is the commander-in-chief of this traitor? Who is the leader of this traitor? Then it would not be wrong,” he added.Bhatia cited the report’s references to Indian Alliance Paris, a France-based organisation, alleging that it was among the first to share videos and amplify social media posts concerning Gandhi’s detention during a protest. He questioned whether the organisation’s activities indicated an attempt by foreign-based groups to influence the narrative around India’s domestic political affairs.“This Progressive International organisation describes itself as a transnational anti-capitalist organisation. According to the report I showed, the unrest and vandalism of historical monuments in France, the incidents in Spain, what is happening in India, and the events in Albania are all linked to Progressive International", Bhatia claimed, alleging that the events formed part of a coordinated effort to challenge elected governments and constitutional institutions.“Wherever there is an elected government, they want to overthrow it. They want to destroy constitutional institutions such as the Supreme Court and Parliament, as well as historical buildings..,France, Albania, Spain and Delhi protests — everything is linked", He claimed, referring to a Congress social media post documenting a meeting between Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and a delegation from the organisation at 10 Janpath in New Delhi in April, 2025.“Rahul Gandhi... Rahul the ‘Gaddar’? Does he not have any strength left in him anymore, that now he has to take the help of such agencies and organisations that are anti-India?” Bhatia said.Bhatia also referred to a social media post by Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut about protests in Albania, alleging that it could be interpreted as support for actions against constitutional institutions. He linked this to slogans raised by protesters on the Supreme Court premises, which he claimed were part of a broader attempt to undermine democratic institutions.“Protesting is a fundamental right, but destruction, destroying institutions, arson, and violent demonstrations are not fundamental rights,” Bhatia said.He demanded that Rahul Gandhi and the Congress disclose what was discussed during the meeting with Progressive International, clarify whether any agreement had been reached and explain the sources of funding for the organisations, including whether they had links with foreign individuals or entities.The Fox News Digital report, titled Global Chaos Inc Grows to 101 Groups, also referred to an international coalition of 28 communist and socialist youth organisations allegedly mobilising students for coordinated strikes across Europe. It said the network extended to the US, UK, Greece, Brazil and India, with groups mobilising supporters, calling strikes and amplifying demonstrations through international media outlets.The report also cited the Neville Roy Singham network and Indian Alliance Paris as alleged amplifiers of French demonstrations on social media, drawing parallels with student protests in India. The claims of coordinated efforts to influence protests in India were not independently established by the material cited at the press conference.Bhatia also criticised Rahul’s interactions with British MP Jeremy Corbyn and US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, alleging that their positions on Kashmir were contrary to India’s interests. He accused Rahul of seeking support from organisations he described as anti-India. "Such organisations may be anti-India, but how can the LoP of the country India be anti-India?", he asked.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Wisconsin priest began a 1920 memorial for three local World War I casualties; over the next decade, Dickeyville’s parish grounds grew into a garden of shrines and grottoes
articles.summary: Explore the captivating history of the Dickeyville Grotto in Wisconsin, a remarkable outdoor folk art site created by Father Matthias Wernerus to honor three local men lost in World War I, blending religious devotion and patriotic tribute.
articles.body: Towns all around America erected memorials to the young men who never returned home following World War I, and the majority of these were straightforward bronze or stone structures. A German-born parish priest in the southwest Wisconsin community of Dickeyville began in a similar manner and continued. In the years that followed, the churchyard of Holy Ghost Parish developed into a garden of concrete shrines and grottos covered in glass, shells, and stones after Father Matthias Wernerus constructed a traditional memorial for three local men who had lost their lives in the conflict. It is still one of the most well-known examples of outdoor folk art in the Midwest and is now called the Dickeyville Grotto.The Wisconsin Historical Society describes it as the state’s most famous and perhaps most striking example of outdoor folk art, tracing its origins to 1919. Wernerus served as parish pastor from 1918 until his death in 1931. State cemetery records show that the statues of the memorial’s Crucifixion Group were purchased in 1920 and that the cemetery layout was changed that year to accommodate them.From monument to grottoWernerus was born in Germany in 1873 and came to Wisconsin in 1904 to study at St. Francis Seminary. A few years later, he was ordained. His initial experiments were small. He decorated flower pots with coloured glass near the memorial. He also urged parishioners to help beautify the parish grounds. In 1924, he began work on the Grotto of the Holy Eucharist. The parish says most of the major work was done between 1925 and 1930.The parish describes the theme as the unity of two ideals, love of God and love of country, which is why the garden mixes religious shrines with a patriotic one. Wernerus himself wrote that many reasons urged him to put up “Religion in Stone and Patriotism in Stone”, and he added that the main reason was one he could not reveal. The patriotic shrine features Columbus, Washington and Lincoln in a colourful setting of stonework. Building something on this scale without blueprints took more than one pair of hands.Concrete, glass and found objectsSAH Archipedia, the online guide to American structures from the Society of Architectural Historians, says Wernerus worked with his cousin, Mary Wernerus, and a worker named George Splinter. At times they poured concrete into wooden forms on stone foundations, erecting pedestals, archways and shrines with about 6,000 bags of cement and six or seven carloads of stone. Then Wernerus decorated the surfaces with fossils, shells, rose quartz, petrified sequoia and cedar, tufa, stalagmites and stalactites. He achieved some of his most unusual effects with glass.The parish’s own brochure mentions plenty more, from coral, amber glass, agate and onyx to petrified wood and the circular knobs once used on the gearsticks of early automobiles. Visitors pass through a Roman arch, into which three rosaries are worked, and enter the main grotto.Wernerus’s work also reflected a wider Catholic trend towards shrine-building, inspired by the visions at Lourdes and Pope Leo XIII’s replica of the Lourdes grotto in the Vatican Gardens. Some have suggested that the Grotto of the Redemption in Iowa also influenced him, but no recorded account confirms that connection.What happened after WernerusSPACES, an archive documenting art environments, records that Wernerus died of pneumonia in February 1931, after which work on the grotto ceased. The site altered little, but in 1964 a succeeding parish priest, Father Lambert Marx, built concrete and sandstone Stations of the Cross.Wernerus had been anxious about the grotto’s future. Susan Niles, who analysed his letters to his bishop, concluded that he expected the grotto to become a major pilgrimage site, and feared that it would become a location of commercial attractions. The parish has largely prevented that outcome, and the grounds at 305 West Main Street remain open for self-guided walking tours.What began as a memorial for three men from one small parish became a landmark attracting visitors from far beyond Grant County. Its evolution into a garden of shrines and grottoes shows how one act of remembrance, carried forward by a priest, his cousin, a helper and a congregation willing to contribute their possessions, developed into an enduring example of outdoor folk art.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2006, a New York couple took a $400,000 mortgage; after the husband died and a years-long foreclosure battle continued, an October 21 court overturned the order to sell the property
articles.summary: A New York mortgage foreclosure case that began more than a decade ago has taken another turn after an appeals court overturned an order directing the
articles.body: A New York mortgage foreclosure case that began more than a decade ago has taken another turn after an appeals court overturned an order directing the sale of a residential property. On October 21, 2026, the New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department, reversed a 2025 foreclosure judgment in Bank of America, N.A. v. Maddox. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia, the dispute involved a $400,000 promissory note signed by Michael McNamara in 2006; his wife, Alice, also signing the mortgage on their Babylon, New York, home. After Michael died in 2010, the foreclosure proceedings continued, with the appeals court ultimately finding that the bank had not adequately established its compliance with mandatory notice requirements or its legal standing to bring the case.A $400,000 mortgage and a foreclosure caseThe case began with a mortgage secured by residential property in Babylon. According to the appellate court’s decision, Michael McNamara signed a $400,000 promissory note in favour of American Brokers Conduit on January 23, 2006. Both Michael and Alice McNamara executed the mortgage. The bank alleged that the couple defaulted by failing to make monthly payments due from May 1, 2009, onwards. Michael died on September 9, 2010, leaving the dispute to continue with Alice involved in the proceedings.In January 2014, Bank of America, N.A., commenced a foreclosure action against the borrowers and other defendants. Alice contested the case, raising several legal defences, including that the bank had not established its standing to sue and had failed to comply with New York’s statutory requirements for notifying borrowers before beginning foreclosure proceedings.Lower court rulings favoured the bankIn July 2018, the Supreme Court in Suffolk County granted key parts of the bank’s motion for summary judgment against Alice. It rejected her relevant defences concerning standing and notice compliance and referred the matter to a referee to calculate the amount owed. In March 2020, the lower court confirmed the referee’s report and issued a judgment of foreclosure and sale, directing that the property be sold. That judgment was subsequently vacated by the lower court on April 30, 2024.However, the proceedings did not end there. On June 23, 2025, the court issued another order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, again directing the sale of the property. Alice’s appeals continued, and after her death, Robert Maddox, acting as executor of her estate, was substituted for her in the case. The appeals court’s October 2026 decision therefore addressed the later foreclosure judgment as well as the procedural status of the earlier appeals.Why the appeals court reversed the foreclosure judgmentThe central issue was whether Bank of America had demonstrated that it fulfilled the legal requirements necessary to obtain summary judgment against Alice. Under Section 1304 of New York’s Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law, a lender generally must provide borrowers with a prescribed notice at least 90 days before commencing a mortgage foreclosure action. The notice must be sent by registered or certified mail and by first-class mail to the required addresses. The appeals court concluded that Alice was entitled to this notice even though she had not signed the underlying promissory note. She had signed the mortgage as a borrower, was identified as a borrower in the document and had agreed under the mortgage terms to pay amounts due under the note.The court also found that the bank had not adequately proved compliance with the notice requirement. An affidavit submitted by a bank officer relied on a review of business records but did not establish personal knowledge of the mailings or sufficiently describe the procedures used to ensure that notices were correctly addressed and sent. Although evidence of certified-mail delivery was submitted, the bank had not established that the required notice was also sent by first-class mail more than 90 days before the action began. The court therefore held that the bank had failed to establish its compliance with Section 1304.The bank also failed to establish standingA second major issue concerned the bank’s legal standing to bring the foreclosure action. In mortgage cases, a lender must establish that it held or had been assigned the underlying promissory note when the action commenced. The appeals court found that the record did not show that a copy of the endorsed note had been attached to the original complaint. It also concluded that the bank officer’s statements about the bank’s possession of the note were based on unidentified business records that had not been produced. The court treated those assertions as inadmissible hearsay and found that the bank had not established its standing.Consequently, the court reversed the June 23, 2025, foreclosure judgment and denied the relevant branches of the bank’s motion for summary judgment. It also awarded one bill of costs to Robert Maddox as executor of Alice’s estate. The ruling does not establish that the mortgage debt never existed or that the property can never be subject to foreclosure. Rather, it means the bank did not establish the necessary legal grounds for the relief granted in these proceedings. The decision highlights how strict compliance with borrower-notification rules and proof of a lender’s standing can determine the outcome of a foreclosure case, even after years of litigation.You use AI every day. articles.title: After months of coyote complaints, toddler bitten in LA neighbourhood; DNA links attack to euthanised animal
articles.summary: A 16-month-old child was bitten by a coyote in Los Angeles’ Atwater Village neighbourhood, prompting renewed scrutiny of months of complaints about the
articles.body: A 16-month-old child was bitten by a coyote in Los Angeles’ Atwater Village neighbourhood, prompting renewed scrutiny of months of complaints about the animal’s presence and behaviour. The incident occurred on October 16 on the 3300 block of Glenhurst Avenue, according to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). Wildlife officers later located a coyote in the same area and euthanised it. DNA testing subsequently confirmed that the animal was responsible for the attack, officials said on October 20. The child was taken to a hospital, treated and released. The incident has raised questions among residents about whether earlier action could have prevented the encounter, with neighbours saying they had repeatedly alerted authorities to concerns about the coyote.Months of coyote complaints preceded toddler's attack in LAResidents told the Los Angeles Times that the coyote had been a concern in the neighbourhood since at least January, when they alleged that a neighbour began feeding the animal. They said it subsequently began approaching homes, entering yards and appearing around residents and their pets.Several neighbours described encounters that they considered threatening. One resident said the coyote chased his cat up a tree, while others said they had stopped allowing their pets outdoors because they feared the animal might attack them.Residents said they had contacted Los Angeles Animal Services and state wildlife officials about the coyote from around June. Richard Dean, one of the residents who raised concerns, shared an email dated June 19 in which he warned city officials that someone could be seriously hurt if the situation continued.Dan Bree, another resident, said neighbours had been trying to get authorities to address the issue for months. The toddler's injury prompted renewed criticism from residents who questioned why the animal had remained in the area despite repeated reports.DNA testing confirms coyote was responsible for attackThe CDFW confirmed on October 20 that DNA samples collected from the child and the euthanised coyote matched, establishing that the animal was responsible for the attack. Wildlife officers had located the coyote near the scene on the evening of October 16 and euthanised it.The confirmation resolved the question of whether the animal captured by officials was the one involved in the incident. The child was treated at a local hospital and subsequently released, according to the department.However, the DNA results did not establish whether the euthanised coyote was the same animal residents had nicknamed “Wiley”, which had reportedly been seen around Atwater Village for months. CBS Los Angeles reported that the identification remained unclear.Allegations of feeding coyote remain under scrutinySome residents alleged that a neighbour had been feeding the coyote, potentially making it more accustomed to human presence. They said they had asked the individual to stop, but the allegations have not been established as a legal finding.Joe Marconi, who lives across the street from the person identified in the complaints, told the Los Angeles Times that he had raised concerns after seeing the coyote near his young daughter and chasing his cat. Other residents also described encounters they considered worrying.Rebecca Dmytryk, chief executive of Humane Wildlife Control, said she had filed a complaint with the state on July 28. Her complaint described a coyote reportedly spending time in a resident's backyard and following people, behaviour she associated with an animal conditioned to expect food from humans.California prohibits feeding non-domesticated mammalian predators, including coyotes. However, authorities said evidence of a violation had not been established during their earlier investigation. The state said it was investigating residents' allegations of intentional feeding.What authorities said about earlier complaintsLos Angeles Animal Services said it had responded to complaints and coordinated with state wildlife officials. According to the department, an animal control officer visited the property of the person identified in the complaints on May 20. The individual denied feeding the coyote, and the officer did not find evidence warranting a violation.The department said further complaints arrived in June and that officers contacted complainants, provided information about coyote behaviour and consulted with the state agency responsible for wildlife management.CDFW also acknowledged receiving tips about suspected illegal feeding. According to the Los Angeles Times, state officials said wildlife officers followed up on the reports but would not attempt to capture the coyote unless an incident such as an attack had occurred.The differing accounts have fuelled residents' concerns about how wildlife agencies respond when coyotes repeatedly approach people. Although the reporting documents complaints made before the attack, it does not establish that earlier intervention would certainly have prevented the incident.Why coyotes can become accustomed to peopleCoyotes are adaptable wild animals that can survive in urban environments, where food, water and shelter may be readily available. Wildlife specialists warn that feeding them, intentionally or unintentionally, can encourage them to associate people with food.This process, known as food conditioning, can make coyotes more likely to approach people in search of food. Habituation, in which animals become less responsive to people after repeated exposure, is a related but distinct process.Dmytryk said she believed the coyote was unusually comfortable around people. However, the publicly reported DNA findings establish the animal's involvement in the bite, not the precise cause of its behaviour.The incident has renewed debate over how urban communities can coexist with wildlife while reducing the risk of encounters involving children and pets.Coyote attacks on people are rare but documentedAttacks on humans are uncommon, but California has recorded incidents involving children. In 1981, three-year-old Kelly Keen was killed by a coyote in Glendale, in what is widely cited as the state's first confirmed fatal coyote attack.Other reported incidents include a coyote biting a six-year-old child at a baseball field in 2025 and an attack involving a child in Woodland Hills in 2022, according to the Los Angeles Times. These cases highlight the potential risks when coyotes come into close contact with people, particularly young children.Wildlife authorities advise residents not to approach or feed coyotes, to secure rubbish and other potential food sources, and to keep children and pets close when an animal is nearby.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI agents raise alarm at US banks over unauthorised access: Report
articles.summary: Major US banks, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, are restricting third-party artificial intelligence (AI) agents
articles.body: Major US banks, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, are restricting third-party artificial intelligence (AI) agents from accessing their platforms amid concerns that unvetted technology could compromise customer accounts and carry out unauthorised financial transactions, Axios reported.The concerns stem from instances in which AI agents accessed customers' accounts using their login credentials and, in some cases, appeared to take actions independently of users' instructions, people familiar with the matter told Axios.AI agents are designed to perform tasks on behalf of users, including accessing financial information and making transactions. However, banks are struggling to distinguish between authorised, user-directed activity and potentially rogue agents, raising concerns about the security of customers' money.Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party AI agents from accessing its platforms, according per reports. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting such access.A Chase spokesperson advised customers against sharing their login credentials with others. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson, meanwhile, said the bank had not observed instances of "rogue AI agents accessing our platforms".Bank executives are particularly concerned about agents that have been granted permission to make purchases or transfer funds, as such access could expose customers to financial losses if the technology acts beyond their instructions.Several banks are considering or moving towards allowing third-party AI agents read-only access, which would let them retrieve customers' financial information without making transactions. Banks already provide similar access to third-party applications, including budgeting services such as Quicken.Despite the security concerns, financial institutions recognise that customers are likely to increasingly rely on AI agents to manage their finances. Banks are therefore looking for ways to accommodate the technology while preventing unauthorised access and transactions.The rapid development of AI tools is making the task more difficult, with banking executives acknowledging that existing systems may not reliably identify whether account activity is being carried out by a customer, an authorised AI agent or an agent acting independently.You use AI every day. articles.title: Psychology explains why some people struggle to say no even when they are exhausted; what people-pleasing reveals about boundaries, approval and the fear of disappointing others
articles.summary: You have had a long day, your own work is unfinished, and you barely have the energy to rest.
articles.body: You have had a long day, your own work is unfinished, and you barely have the energy to rest. Then a colleague asks you to take on another task, a friend needs a favour or a family member expects you to make time for them. You want to say no, but instead you hear yourself saying, “Okay, I’ll manage.” For some people, this happens so often that they end up exhausted, frustrated and sometimes resentful of the very people they wanted to help. They know they have taken on too much, yet turning down the next request still feels uncomfortable.Psychologists describe this pattern as people-pleasing: repeatedly putting other people’s needs ahead of your own, even when doing so comes at a personal cost. It is not simply about being kind or considerate. The difficulty begins when a person feels that keeping others happy is more important than protecting their own time, energy or preferences.A 2026 study published in Current Psychology developed and tested a measure of people-pleasing in two samples of 571 and 1,323 participants. The researchers identified three key dimensions: feeling responsible, neglecting one’s own needs and prioritising other people’s expectations.Why does saying no feel so difficult?One reason is the fear of disappointing someone. A person may worry that declining a request will make them seem selfish, unreliable or uncaring. Instead of treating a request as something they can consider, they may feel pressure to agree to preserve the relationship. Research on people-pleasing suggests that some people use agreeableness to avoid conflict, rejection or isolation. A 2025 study developed and tested a questionnaire among 2,203 Chinese university students. It examined people-pleasing through thoughts, behaviours and feelings, highlighting that the pattern involves more than simply doing favours for others.This can help explain why someone may say yes even when they know they cannot manage another responsibility. The immediate discomfort of refusing may feel harder to tolerate than the tiredness that comes later.When approval becomes more important than your own needsPeople-pleasing can also be linked to how a person measures their own worth. If being helpful earns praise, affection or approval, they may begin to associate saying yes with being a good friend, partner, child or employee. Over time, the person may find it difficult to distinguish between wanting to help and feeling that they must help. They might agree to plans they do not want, take responsibility for work that belongs to someone else or apologise simply because another person is upset.The 2026 study found that people-pleasing was related to traits such as agreeableness, empathy and emotionality, but was distinct from them. In other words, caring about others does not automatically mean someone is a people-pleaser. The defining feature is the tendency to put others’ needs first at the expense of one’s own.Why the habit can leave people exhaustedThe problem is not one extra favour or a single difficult week. It is the repeated experience of accepting more than a person can reasonably manage. Someone who rarely declines requests may have less time for sleep, exercise, relationships or unfinished personal tasks. They may also feel frustrated when others continue to ask for help without realising how much pressure they are under.The 2026 research discusses emotional exhaustion as a possible consequence of taking on additional responsibilities while neglecting personal needs. However, the study does not establish that people-pleasing directly causes exhaustion in every person. The pattern can also make relationships less honest. If someone routinely agrees when they want to refuse, other people may never realise that the arrangement is unfair or unsustainable.How to start saying no without feeling guiltySaying no does not require becoming less caring. It means recognising that another person’s disappointment does not automatically make your decision wrong.Pause before agreeing: If someone asks you for a favour, resist the urge to say yes immediately. Say, “Let me check my schedule first.” This gives you time to consider your workload, energy and other commitments before making a decision.Keep your refusal short and clear: You do not need to offer a long explanation every time you decline a request. A simple “I won’t be able to manage this today” is enough. Overexplaining can make you feel that you need the other person’s permission to say no.Stop treating disappointment as rejection: Someone may be disappointed when you cannot help, but that does not necessarily mean they are angry with you or that the relationship is in trouble. Allowing others to have their feelings without immediately trying to fix them can make it easier to maintain boundaries.Offer help only when you genuinely can: If you want to help but cannot take on the entire task, suggest a smaller alternative. For example, say, “I can help you for 15 minutes, but I can’t handle the whole thing.” Do this only if you have the time and energy; a boundary should not become another obligation.Practise saying no in low-pressure situations: Start with small requests that you would ordinarily accept out of habit, such as an invitation you do not want to attend or an extra task you cannot fit into your day. Each time, remind yourself that declining a request is not the same as rejecting a person.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: In a first, Australia's Ghost Shark submarine turns into aerial drone launchpad
articles.summary: Australia's Ghost Shark has revealed a new dimension of underwater warfare, launching aerial drones from its uncrewed submarine in a first-of-its-kind
articles.body: Australia's Ghost Shark has revealed a new dimension of underwater warfare, launching aerial drones from its uncrewed submarine in a first-of-its-kind demonstration that could give underwater platforms the ability to extend their reach into the skies.According to The War Zone (TWZ), footage released by manufacturer Anduril shows Ghost Shark surfacing, opening its upper hull compartments and raising a launcher containing 12 angled tubes to deploy an ALTIUS-type aerial drone. The demonstration offers a glimpse of how autonomous underwater vehicles could carry and launch aerial assets for surveillance and strike missions.Australia's defence industry minister Pat Conroy said the Ghost Shark programme is being developed to expand the Royal Australian Navy's autonomous undersea warfare capabilities.On October 19, the Australian government disclosed three planned payload roles for the platform: deploying up to 12 sea mines, placing logistics caches on the seabed and launching aerial drones for surveillance and strike missions.The latest footage also reveals two retractable masts on Ghost Shark, offering new clues about how the underwater vehicle could communicate with its aerial drones. One larger mast rises from the centre of the hull and carries an antenna, while a smaller mast extends vertically from a separate compartment towards the rear.According to TWZ, these systems could potentially support direct communication with the drones or satellite links, allowing operators to receive surveillance data and coordinate missions remotely. However, their exact functions have not been confirmed.Inside Ghost Shark submarine and the ALTIUS dronesThe Ghost Shark is an extra-large autonomous underwater vehicle developed by Anduril Australia for the Royal Australian Navy. Its modular design allows it to carry different mission-specific payloads, including sea mines, seabed logistics caches and ALTIUS uncrewed aerial vehicles.The submarine is designed to conduct extended underwater missions without a crew onboard, potentially allowing Australia to undertake dangerous operations while reducing risks to sailors.The newly released footage shows Ghost Shark surfacing and raising a launcher containing 12 angled tubes to fire an ALTIUS-type aerial drone. The exact variant has not been confirmed, but the ALTIUS-600 is designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, while the ALTIUS-600M is configured for strike missions.According to Anduril, the ALTIUS-600 has a maximum range of around 275 miles (442 km) and an endurance of at least four hours.The launcher could allow Ghost Shark to deploy multiple aerial drones during a single mission, extending its reach beyond its own underwater sensors. Depending on the drone configuration, these aircraft could gather intelligence, monitor maritime activity or conduct attacks.

articles.title: Karva Chauth 2026 date: October 28 or 29? Check the correct date, puja muhurat and moonrise time
articles.summary: If you’ve been scrolling through social media or Google, trying to figure out whether Karva Chauth falls on October 28 or October 29 this year, you can
articles.body: If you’ve been scrolling through social media or Google, trying to figure out whether Karva Chauth falls on October 28 or October 29 this year, you can stop second-guessing yourself.For everyone celebrating in India, the fast takes place on Thursday, October 29, 2026.The confusion pops up every year because of how lunar calendars work compared to standard dates. In 2026, the Chaturthi tithi doesn't kick in until 1:06 AM on October 29, running straight through to 10:09 PM that night. Because the moonrise falls within that window in India, October 29 is the official day. (If you saw October 28 online, that’s meant for people living in Western time zones like North America, where the time shift pulls the date back).Key timings you need to knowHere’s how the day breaks down for New Delhi (though local times shift slightly depending on where you're based):Date: Thursday, October 29, 2026 Fast Begins (Sunrise): Around 6:30 AM Puja Muhurat: 5:38 PM to 6:56 PM Expected Moonrise: Around 8:17 PM If you live in a different major city, your moonrise time will vary:Lucknow: ~8:06 PM Kolkata: ~7:47 PM Mumbai: ~9:00 PM Bengaluru: ~8:55 PM How the day unfoldsFor those observing the traditional nirjala (waterless) fast for their partner's long life and well-being, the routine starts early.You’ll wake up before dawn to eat sargi - the pre-fast meal traditionally prepared by mothers-in-law. Finish off your dry fruits, mathri, and water before the sun rises around 6:30 AM, because once daylight breaks, no food or drink passes your lips until the moon comes out.Later in the afternoon, during the evening muhurat (starting around 5:38 PM), women gather for the Karva Chauth puja, dress in festive clothes, and pass around the thalis while listening to the vrat katha.Breaking the fastThe hardest part of the day is usually the final stretch waiting for the moon.Once the moon clears the horizon, you offer arghya (water) through a sieve, look at your partner, and finally take that first sip of water to officially break the fast. Just keep in mind that urban high-rises, smog, or clouds can delay your view by 10 to 15 minutes past the official moonrise time!Lock in October 29 on your calendar, double-check your city’s exact panchang timings, and get your sargi prep sorted ahead of time.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Psychology explains why some couples can sit together in silence without feeling awkward while others need constant conversation; what this means about emotional security, intimacy and relationship expectations
articles.summary: A couple can spend an entire evening sitting together without saying much, yet feel completely connected.
articles.body: A couple can spend an entire evening sitting together without saying much, yet feel completely connected. Another couple might experience the same silence as uncomfortable, wondering whether something is wrong or whether their partner has lost interest. This difference is not necessarily about how much two people love each other. Psychology suggests that the meaning behind silence, along with each partner’s emotional needs and expectations, can shape how comfortable they feel together.A study published in the journal Motivation and Emotion in 2024 examined silence in romantic relationships across four studies. Researchers explored how the reasons behind these quiet moments influenced people’s emotions, psychological needs and feelings of closeness. The findings suggest that silence can strengthen a relationship when it is freely chosen and enjoyed but can create discomfort when it comes from anxiety, pressure or hostility.When silence becomes a sign of emotional securityIn the early stages of a relationship, conversations often help two people learn about each other. Partners ask questions, share stories and look for common interests. As familiarity grows, however, they may no longer feel the need to fill every moment with words. For some couples, sitting together quietly becomes a natural part of being close. One person might read a book while the other listens to music, or both might relax after a long day without feeling obliged to start a conversation.Such moments can reflect emotional security. Partners feel comfortable enough to be themselves without worrying that every pause will be misunderstood. They do not need to entertain each other constantly or prove their affection through continuous conversation. The 2024 study found that silence motivated by a genuine desire to be close was associated with more positive feelings and stronger relationship closeness. These moments were often linked to calm, peaceful emotions rather than excitement.However, comfortable silence is not a universal measure of a successful relationship. Some couples express closeness through frequent conversation, humour and sharing everyday details. Others enjoy spending time together with fewer words. Neither pattern is automatically better than the other.Why some people feel the need to keep talkingNot everyone experiences silence in the same way. For some people, conversation is an important way of feeling connected, reassured and included in their partner’s life. When the conversation suddenly stops, they may wonder whether their partner is upset, distracted or emotionally distant. They might begin asking questions simply to restore a sense of connection. Personal communication habits, past experiences and expectations about relationships can all influence these reactions. Someone who values regular verbal reassurance may interpret silence differently from a partner who feels loved through physical presence or practical support.This does not necessarily mean that the more talkative partner is insecure or that the quieter partner is emotionally mature. It simply shows that people can have different ways of experiencing intimacy. The important question is whether both partners feel understood. If one person needs conversation to feel connected while the other prefers quiet time, acknowledging these differences can help prevent unnecessary misunderstandings.Not all silence means the same thingWhile comfortable silence can bring partners closer, quietness can also signal an unresolved problem. The difference often lies in the reason for staying silent and the feelings surrounding it. The researchers distinguished between silence that comes naturally from a desire for closeness and silence driven by internal pressure or external motives, such as wanting to punish or shut out a partner. For example, a couple relaxing together without speaking may feel peaceful and connected. In contrast, one partner refusing to respond after an argument to make the other feel guilty can create emotional distance.Silence can also occur when someone is afraid to express an opinion because they expect criticism, rejection or conflict. In such cases, the absence of conversation may reflect discomfort rather than security. The study linked anxiety-driven and hostile forms of silence with less positive emotions and poorer relationship experiences. This highlights why the number of words exchanged is not enough to judge the health of a relationship. A quiet evening does not automatically mean something is wrong, just as constant conversation does not guarantee emotional closeness. The surrounding circumstances and each partner’s experience matter.How couples can understand each other betterPartners do not have to share identical communication styles to build a strong relationship. What matters is making room for both people’s needs without treating their differences as evidence that something is wrong. If one partner enjoys quiet time while the other prefers talking, they can discuss what helps each of them feel connected. A simple conversation about whether silence feels relaxing or uncomfortable can prevent assumptions from turning into resentment.It is equally important to recognise when quietness follows an argument or becomes a repeated way of avoiding difficult conversations. Taking time to calm down can be helpful, but explaining the need for space and returning to the discussion later can reassure both partners. Ultimately, intimacy is not measured by how often a couple speaks. It can develop through meaningful conversations, shared activities, attentive listening and peaceful moments together.The most useful distinction is whether silence feels freely chosen and comfortable or whether it leaves one or both partners feeling ignored, anxious or unable to speak honestly. When couples understand what their silence means to each other, they can build a connection that allows room for both conversation and quiet companionship.You use AI every day.
